question: How does fire spread on fabric in microgravity?
answer: When a thin fuel is ignited in the middle under low forced-flow velocities in microgravity, the flame spreads upstream into the oncoming airflow [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. In contrast, flames in normal gravity spread downstream in the direction of buoyant flow [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. Spacecraft experiments evaluated fabric combustion using Nomex, Ultem, and a fuel blend of 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass [PSI-26 · doi:10.60555/58h4-dy80]. During these tests, airflow was directed along the fuel surface in opposed or concurrent directions at speeds up to 40 cm/s [PSI-26 · doi:10.60555/58h4-dy80]. Materials can also burn at lower oxygen levels in microgravity than on Earth [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. Our sources do not cover specific numerical flame spread rates for fabrics in microgravity [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science][PSI-26 · doi:10.60555/58h4-dy80].

question: Which experiments tested oxygen levels above 30%?
answer:
Four NASA PSI experiments tested oxygen levels above 30% [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row]. 

- PSI-159 ACME CFI-G tested oxygen levels ranging from 12% to 85% [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row][PSI-159 · doi:10.60555/cyt1-kh64].
- PSI-10 ACME/Flame Design tested oxygen levels from 19.8048% to 84.9978% [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row][PSI-10 · doi:10.60555/w4zy-bt45].
- PSI-20 ACME BRE tested oxygen levels between 21% and 40% [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row][PSI-20 · doi:10.60555/vb93-3y72].
- PSI-69 FLEX tested oxygen levels from 12% to 34% [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row].

Our sources do not report oxygen levels for several other experiments, specifically PSI-21, PSI-22, PSI-26, PSI-47, PSI-60, PSI-62, PSI-100, PSI-101, PSI-102, PSI-106, PSI-107, PSI-115, PSI-117, and PSI-142 [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row].

question: How was smoke detection tested on the ISS, and why does it matter?
answer:
Smoke detection on the ISS was tested using the Dust Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test to measure background aerosol levels and the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) to examine smoke particle sizes from spacecraft materials [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. In the SAME experiment, solid fuels such as Teflon, Kapton, and Silicone Rubber were tested using Comparative Soot Diagnostic Hardware under an airflow of 5–10 cm/s across 4 experimental test rows [PSI-102 · doi:10.60555/gd4k-8h62]. 

This testing matters because microgravity alters buoyancy and particle growth, producing larger smoke particles that can change detector responses or prevent alarms from triggering [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science][PSI-102 · doi:10.60555/gd4k-8h62]. Quantitative data from these tests provides a microgravity baseline to evaluate existing detectors and create reliable fire-detection technology for long-duration space missions and extreme Earth environments like submarines [PSI-101 · doi:10.60555/2np7-jv14][PSI-102 · doi:10.60555/gd4k-8h62][PSI-47 · doi:10.60555/ztgj-d202].

question: What gases were used to put out flames, and in which experiment?
answer:
Nitrogen gas was applied as a suppressant to extinguish flames in a drop tower test burning a PMMA sphere [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. Nitrogen was also used as a flame suppressant in early microgravity combustion testing [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. Additionally, the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) evaluated and used gaseous fire suppressants including carbon dioxide, helium, sulfur hexafluoride (SF6), and nitrogen [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science][PSI-69 · doi:10.60555/mbq8-0451]. 

Our sources do not cover the specific identity of the gas used in the BASS experiment, stating only that an inert gaseous extinguishing agent was assessed [PSI-26 · doi:10.60555/58h4-dy80].

question: What happened in the Mir fire in 1997, and what was learned?
answer:
On February 24, 1997, a fire ignited in a solid fuel oxygen generator inside the Kvant-1 module of the space station Mir [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir]. The searing flame lasted several minutes, cut off access to one of the two Soyuz escape vehicles, and filled station modules with toxic smoke [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir]. The six crew members extinguished the fire with no structural damage to the station, and the life support system cleared the smoke over several hours with no lasting harm to the crew [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir]. 

Lessons learned from the incident were applied to the design and operations of the International Space Station [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir]. Russian space officials updated emergency training for crew members, altered ground controller responses, and changed the ground preparation of generator canisters [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir]. Additionally, the International Space Station implemented redundant oxygen generation systems, keeping an updated solid fuel oxygen generator with extra safety measures as a backup [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir].

question: Is there any fire data for Moon or Mars gravity?
answer: The NASA PSI Data Repository contains no combustion data from real Moon or Mars gravity [PSI Combustion Science coverage (24 investigations) · psi.nasa.gov/physci/repo/search?q=combustion]. The closest PSI investigation, PSI-22, used an electric field to mimic partial gravity [PSI Combustion Science coverage (24 investigations) · psi.nasa.gov/physci/repo/search?q=combustion]. Simulated lunar gravity fire data exists from a drop tower centrifuge experiment showing solid fabric burning in air [NASA Combustion Science · nasa.gov/glenn/glenn-expertise-space-exploration/physical-sciences-program/combustion-science]. Additionally, the Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2) experiment is planned to investigate burning materials in lunar gravity on another planetary body [NASA Combustion Science · nasa.gov/glenn/glenn-expertise-space-exploration/physical-sciences-program/combustion-science]. The provided sources do not cover any fire data specifically for Mars gravity [PSI Combustion Science coverage (24 investigations) · psi.nasa.gov/physci/repo/search?q=combustion].

question: What are cool flames and why are they a risk?
answer:
Cool flames are a low-temperature combustion regime that form as an intermediate step between unreacted fuel and oxidizer [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. Cool diffusion flames have peak temperatures of 500 to 1000 K [PSI-159 · doi:10.60555/cyt1-kh64]. They can form after a visible flame extinguishes and can burn for a prolonged period of time while burning only a fraction of the vaporized fuel [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. 

Cool flames pose a risk because reduced-gravity environments in space are particularly conducive to low-temperature combustion, creating spacecraft fire safety concerns [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science][PSI-39 · doi:10.60555/m6pj-a914]. Their ability to persist undetected after visible hot flame extinction also impacts fire safety [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. 

The sources do not cover specific terrestrial hazard risks or detailed physical damage mechanisms caused by cool flames beyond spacecraft fire safety concerns [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science][PSI-39 · doi:10.60555/m6pj-a914].
